1:
The chapter opens on the bare formula of resumption, and the witnesses read the small phrase as a study in Elihu’s manner. The reformed John Gill supposes a considerable pause: Elihu had left Job free to reply or object, and only when he perceived that Job was not inclined to answer did he go on; this fresh instalment is called an answer not because Job had said anything for him to answer, but because several matters still remained which Elihu had proposed to himself to take up, and now does. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott is sharper about the distance between the profession and the performance: Elihu here hardly makes good the profession with which he starts, for he begins immediately to accuse Job in no measured language, even while making a great parade of wisdom, expressly addressing the wise at v.2 and insisting on the necessity of discrimination at vv.3-4; and he notes, drily, that Job himself had already uttered much the same sentiment about the testing ear back at ch. 12:11, an incidental hint that we are scarcely meant to read the long debate as the record of an actual conversation.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke maps the whole speech in advance, and the map is worth keeping in view: Elihu opens with an exhortation to the bystanders at vv.1-4, charges Job with accusing God of injustice and shows the charge impossible at vv.5-12, sets out the power and judgments of the Almighty at vv.13-30, and closes by showing how men ought to address God and how irreverently Job had acted at vv.31-37. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry watches Elihu the orator working to gain his hearers’ good-will before he strikes: he calls them wise men and men of knowledge, appeals to their judgment and so submits himself to their trial, and takes them into partnership in the search for truth, only then turning to arraign Job for the passionate words that had reflected on the divine government. The voices converge on one portrait: a speaker who claims the calm of an arbiter while already leaning hard toward the prosecution, courteous to the company and severe to the sufferer, confident that the case he is about to press will bear the strictest sifting. The very word answered, Gill had observed, is used here in its looser sense, of a man who takes up a discourse and carries it further, rather than of a reply to anything Job had actually spoken; the speech resumes not because it was interrupted, but because its speaker has more to say.
2:
Elihu’s summons to a hearing turns on the identity of the wise men he addresses, and here the witnesses sift the audience. The reformed John Gill is at pains to say who is not meant: not Job’s three friends, with whom Elihu was displeased for condemning Job without convicting him, and to whom he could scarcely apply flattering titles of wisdom except in irony; rather, some bystanders known to Elihu as men of real knowledge and understanding. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reason to the same conclusion by elimination: the wise and the experienced whose ear he bespeaks are neither Job and the three, who are the very subject of his arbitration, nor everyone capable of forming a judgment, but the circle of spectators and listeners assumed to have gathered round the disputants. They note that Elihu opens afresh, taking up the word as the Septuagint rightly renders the phrase, now that Job is silent.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds only a small gloss with a long reach, that the ear is here put for the mind, to which things are conveyed by it; the summons to hear is a summons to weigh. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the courtesy and its lesson: Elihu speaks as to wise men who can judge what he says, borrowing the apostle’s confidence in 1 Cor. 10:15, and though he differs from them in opinion he still allows them the name of wise and knowing men. Peevish disputants, Henry observes, think all fools who are not of their mind; but it is a piece of justice we owe to the wise to acknowledge them so, even when our sentiments do not agree with theirs. To grant an opponent the credit of wisdom, Henry implies, is itself a mark of the very wisdom Elihu is inviting his hearers to exercise.

So the verse gathers three complementary readings without any real quarrel among them. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch converge, by different roads, on an audience of onlookers rather than the parties to the dispute, and thereby quietly reinforce Ellicott’s suspicion that the scene is framed as a set piece with spectators, not a private wrangle. Wesley fixes the organ of judgment, Henry the manners of it; and all four agree that Elihu, whatever the heat that is to follow, opens by inviting the discerning to try his words, staking his credit on their verdict and modelling the very trial of speech that the next verse will make his rule.
3:
The ground of the appeal is a proverb Elihu had used once already, that the ear tries words as the palate tastes its food, and the witnesses divide gently over how much the figure carries. The reformed John Gill reads it wholly of discernment: the ear tries not merely the musical sound of words, their diction and grammar, but their sense, whether the matter be sound speech that cannot be condemned or unsound, right or wrong, agreeable to right reason, sound doctrine, and the word of God. A sanctified ear tries these; but a man must have such an ear, must hear internally as well as externally, retain what he hears, distinguish good from bad, and hold fast the truth — and this hearing ear, Gill adds, is the gift of the Lord.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke will not let the figure be only moral. He rejects Calmet’s confining it to the inward judgment, and hears in it the Eastern delight in the harmonious collection of words: the Asiatics prized euphony in speaking and writing, and Elihu, Clarke suspects, labours as much for harmonious versification as for weighty and pious sentiment. To connect sense with sound was the general pursuit of the Hebrew, Arabic, and Persian poets, some of the latter so fond of euphony that they sacrifice both sense and sentiment to it, a fault not unknown even to certain of the Greeks. On this reading the tasting ear savours the music of speech as well as its truth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the plainer sense and turns it into a rule of fair dealing: the ear of the judicious tries words, whether what is said be true or false, right or wrong, and he that speaks must stand the test of the intelligent. As we are bound to prove all things we hear, so we must be willing that what we ourselves speak should be proved. The witnesses thus leave the verse with two layers held loosely together. Gill and Henry take the trying of words as the testing of doctrine and truth, the discipline of a mind that will not swallow whatever it is told; Clarke overlays this with the connoisseur’s ear for the fitness of sound to sense. Neither reading cancels the other, and both serve Elihu’s purpose, that his own words, offered to men who know how to listen, are submitted freely to the same assay.
4:
Having asked for the trained ear, Elihu now invites his hearers into a joint search: let us choose to ourselves judgment, and know among ourselves what is good. The reformed John Gill reads the choosing as the taking of sides where truth and justice lie, and doubts not that Elihu has the present controversy with Job in view — the company is to fix on the just part of the question and hold to it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the summons into a caution against the vices of debate: let us not seek the applause of men, nor contend for victory, but let our aim be to obtain correct views and notions of all things, and let us labour to find out what is good. The point of the inquiry is truth, not triumph.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its fullest voice, hearing in it Elihu’s refusal to play the sole dictator. He does not undertake to pronounce by himself what is just and good and what is not, but is willing to join with the others in searching it out and desires a consultation: let us agree to lay aside all animosities and feuds, all prejudice and affectation of contradiction, and all stiffness in adhering to an opinion once espoused; let us fix right principles to proceed upon, take right methods for finding out truth, and by comparing notes and communicating our reasons come to know among ourselves what is good and what is otherwise. We are likeliest to discern what is right, Henry notes, when we agree to assist one another in searching it out.

The three voices do not divide; they lay a single ideal of honest disputation side by side, and the irony of it is not lost on the reader. Elihu proposes a tribunal of candour, a shared and unprejudiced pursuit of the good, at the very threshold of a speech that Ellicott and Clarke will elsewhere find anything but candid toward Job. Yet the ideal itself is sound, and the witnesses commend it: that the end of argument is not to win but to know, that opinions are to be tried by right principles and not clung to for pride’s sake, and that truth is best found by minds willing to weigh together rather than to shout each other down. It is a standard by which Elihu himself, in the verses to come, may fairly be measured.
5:
“For Job hath said, I am righteous: and God hath taken away my judgment” — Elihu now recites the words he means to answer, and the witnesses divide over whether he reports Job fairly or overstates him. The reformed John Gill grants that Job never said it in so many words, though what he said amounted to it, and carefully distinguishes the senses: Job was righteous in the evangelical sense, justified as the Old Testament saints were, upright by God’s own testimony, holy in life; but he never claimed to be righteous in or of himself, or free from sin, which would contradict his own confessions. Yet Gill allows that Job thought himself so righteous that he ought not to have been afflicted as he was, and it is probably in this sense that Elihu understood him.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the defence of Job further. Adam Clarke insists that Job had indeed said such words, as at ch. 27:2, but only in vindication of his aspersed character, and in a quite different sense from that in which Elihu takes them up: he asserted himself righteous only as touching the charges his friends had brought, never that he had always a pure heart. And when Job said God had taken away his judgment, he did not mean to charge God with injustice, but to say that God had dealt with him in a way wholly mysterious, not interposing while his friends overwhelmed him with reproach. John Wesley reads it in the same key: I am so far righteous that I have not deserved such hard usage from God, and God, as at ch. 27:2, denies me that which is just, a fair hearing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, by contrast, records the recital as a real accusation, one Job ought to be checked for: Job had insisted on his own innocency, maintained his plea of not guilty, and, worst of all, charged God with injustice in his dealings, as though God had wronged him and would not right him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply anchors the quotation in the text, pointing back to ch. 13:18 and again to ch. 27:2. So the debate is genuine and turns on a matter of justice to the accused: whether Elihu, in reducing Job’s laments to the flat propositions “I am righteous” and “God hath taken away my judgment,” has caught his real meaning or flattened a sufferer’s protest into a blasphemy he never intended.
6:
The next clause Elihu attributes to Job is a defiant refusal to lie about himself, and beneath it runs a real difficulty of both text and grammar. The reformed John Gill supplies the sense as a question answered: should I lie against my right? No, I ought not; for Job to own himself a wicked man and a hypocrite would be to speak against himself, contrary to conscience, and to do his own character no justice — though Gill notes that some, with Broughton, read the words without the interrogation. On the second clause, “my wound is incurable without transgression,” the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads a plain and pathetic truth: Job is treated as the worst of culprits and labours under incurable maladies, yet without any cause on his part, exactly as God had testified of him in ch. 1:1 and ch. 2:3, that Satan had moved the Lord against him without cause. Clarke lingers over the philology, for the word rendered wound means literally my arrow, the shaft that has struck him, and by various renderings the line yields “a man of calamities without transgression.”

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that reading: the wound is literally the arrow that has wounded him, as at ch. 16:13 and ch. 17:1, and “without transgression” means on Job’s part, as at ch. 16:17. He records the rival construction, “notwithstanding my right, I am accounted a liar,” but judges the Authorized Version’s rendering the more probable. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the strophe and name the axiom Elihu is about to wield: that wickedness and wrong are inconceivable on God’s part — a truth in itself, and the very axiom the three friends defend, but which Elihu will apply more justly than they.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the defence of Job: should I falsely accuse myself of sins of which I am not guilty, of any such crying sin as might reasonably bring down such terrible judgments? The witnesses do not finally divide over the images of arrow and wound; their small quarrel is only over the mood and the rendering — whether the first line is a proud question that refuses a false confession, as Gill and the Authorized Version take it, or the darker complaint “I am reckoned a liar in spite of my right.” What they share is the sense of a man who will not purchase relief by perjuring himself against his own conscience, though the arrow of God is fast in him.
7:
Elihu’s astonishment breaks out in a question, what man is like Job, who drinks up scorning like water, and the witnesses trace both the wonder and the borrowed image. The reformed John Gill hears the marvel at a man once esteemed so wise and good behaving as Job now did — the question is put as though no such example had been seen. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke recognizes the charge as a repetition of one Eliphaz had already flung at ch. 15:16, and unfolds the proverb behind it: the metaphor is from a camel, which at setting out on a journey in the caravan takes in a great draught of water, even the most turbid, to last it through the desert; so Job is said to fill his heart with scorning, drinking it down greedily.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that the same word had been aimed at Job before, by Zophar at ch. 11:3 and by Eliphaz at ch. 15:16; the reproach is not new-minted but recycled from the friends’ earlier speeches, which is itself a quiet mark against Elihu’s claim to break fresh ground. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads “like water” as abundantly and greedily, of a man who breaks forth into scornful expressions not only against his friends but, in some sort, against God himself.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry offers three ways of taking the drinking of scorn, and lets the reader weigh them. Job may be pictured as sitting in the seat of the scornful, taking a great liberty to reproach both God and his friends and finding a pleasure in it; or as greedy in receiving and hearkening to the scorns that others cast upon their brethren, well pleased with such talk and extolling it; or, thirdly, by these foolish expressions he makes himself the object of scorn, lays himself open to reproach, and gives occasion to others to laugh at him, while his religion suffers and its reputation is wounded through his side. Henry turns the last sense into a prayer, that God will never leave us to ourselves to say or do anything that makes us a reproach to the foolish, as the psalmist begs in Ps. 39:8. The witnesses converge on the substance of the charge while parting only over its precise edge — whether Job pours out scorn, drinks in the scorn of others, or draws scorn down upon himself — and none of them fails to notice that Elihu, in framing it, has reached back for a weapon the friends had already used.
8:
The indictment sharpens: Job goes in company with the workers of iniquity and walks with wicked men. Yet the witnesses, almost with one voice, refuse to let the words bear their harshest sense, and read them of opinion rather than of literal company. The reformed John Gill names the company plainly enough — the worst of men, who make sinning their constant trade — but the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke at once softens the charge. Elihu’s assertion, taken strictly, was not true; Job did not consort with profligates. The likelier meaning, drawn out of the Hebrew, is that Job makes a track to join fellowship with the workers of iniquity, in that his present mode of reasoning — I am righteous, yet God hath taken away my judgment — is the very language of sinners who say there is no profit in serving God, since the just man is not vindicated against his oppressors. By adopting so much of their creed, Job is taking the steps that lead toward their fellowship, a point Clarke ties forward to v.9.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that this too was a charge Eliphaz had brought against Job before, at ch. 15:4 and ch. 22:15, so that Elihu is again treading a path already worn. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the moderating reading in a sentence: I dare not say that he is a wicked man, yet in this matter he speaks and acts like one of them. The distinction is exact — not that Job is of the party of the wicked, but that his words, on this one head, march with theirs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the same reading its finest form: Job is here represented as walking in the course of the ungodly and standing in the way of sinners, not that in his conversation he associated with them, but that in his opinion he favoured and countenanced them and strengthened their hands. If, as the next verse alleges, it profits a man nothing to delight himself in God, why should he not lay the reins on the neck of his lusts and herd with the workers of iniquity? A man who says he has cleansed his hands in vain not only offends against the generation of God’s children, as the psalmist feared in Ps. 73:13, but gratifies God’s enemies and says as they say. The witnesses do not divide; they agree, against the letter of the charge, that Job’s fault is not the fellowship of the wicked but a turn of argument that, unguarded, does their cause a service.
9:
The proof of the last charge is the saying Elihu now puts in Job’s mouth, that it profits a man nothing to delight himself with God; and the witnesses agree at once that Job never said it in those terms. The reformed John Gill notes that the words are not Job’s plainly and expressly, but only consequentially, what might be thought to follow from what he had actually said. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same: not in express terms, but by consequence, because Job had said that good men are no less, and sometimes more, miserable here than the wicked. The charge, in short, is an inference, and both witnesses mark it as such rather than as a quotation.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gathers the passages the inference is drawn from, at ch. 9:22 and ch. 10:15, and then turns the tables with a fine stroke. Eliphaz, he observes, had virtually said the same thing, though in the converse form, when he represented it as a matter of indifference to God whether a man is righteous or not, at ch. 22:3; and that was to sap the foundations of all morality, for if God cares not whether a man is righteous, it certainly cannot profit a man to be so. The doctrine Elihu fastens on Job as a scandal is one the friends had themselves let slip.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the saying most carefully, for he will neither excuse nor exaggerate it. To delight ourselves with God, he grants, is the truest notion of religion — communion with him, concurrence with him, walking with him as Enoch did — and its ways are pleasantness; so there is a present pleasure in godliness that no affliction can take away. What is denied, and wrongly, is the advantage of it, as though it were vain to serve God, the very complaint of the murmurers in Mal. 3:14. Henry thinks Job’s words at ch. 9:22, that God destroys the perfect and the wicked, had a truth in them, since all things come alike to all, but were ill expressed and gave too much occasion for this imputation, so that Job sat silent under it rather than excuse himself. The witnesses do not divide: they agree that Elihu presses an inference, not a confession, and that its sting lies precisely in the danger of a hasty word, honestly meant, that lends itself to a meaning the speaker never owned.
10:
“Far be it from God, that he should do wickedness; and from the Almighty, that he should commit iniquity” — with this Elihu turns from accusation to his great thesis, and the witnesses gather round the axiom of divine justice. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets it out both ways: God does wrong to none, for he can no more commit iniquity than he can die, or lie, or deny himself; and he ministers justice to all, rendering to every man according to his work. The truth respects the justice and equity of all God’s proceedings; he never inflicts the evil of punishment but where he finds the evil of sin, nor in any undue proportion, for that would be to pervert judgment. Because he is God, infinitely perfect and holy, he can neither do wrong himself nor countenance it; though Almighty, he never uses his power, as mighty men do, for the support of injustice, but is Shaddai, all-sufficient, and so cannot be tempted with evil to do an unrighteous thing, as the apostle says in James 1:13.

The reformed John Gill notes that Elihu addresses the same persons as men of understanding, of heart, the heart being the seat of wisdom, and desires their attention to a refutation of Job’s sense. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the Hebrew word-order, reading it as an exclamation: wickedness, far be that from God, and iniquity from the Almighty.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks how Elihu now takes broader ground than the three friends. He appeals to men of understanding — hardly the friends, of whom he has spoken slightingly, but an audience real or imagined, set to decide the merits of the case — and he concerns himself not with the problems of God’s government but simply with the impossibility of his acting unjustly, appealing, like Abraham in Gen. 18:25, to the certainty that the Judge of all the earth will do right. The reason Ellicott finds somewhat strange but sound at bottom: God is irresponsible, in the old sense that none has put him in charge over the earth; his authority is ultimate and original, and so he can have no private interest to secure at the creature’s expense, for the welfare of his creatures is the welfare of that which is his own, as the good shepherd of John 10:12 cares for sheep that are truly his. The witnesses do not divide; they lay the foundation of the whole discourse — that whatever we cannot explain in God’s dealings, injustice is not to be thought of, and the fault of any perplexity lies in us, not in him.
11:
The positive side of the axiom is retribution: the work of a man God renders to him, and causes every man to find according to his ways. The reformed John Gill takes it simply, with Ben Gersom, as the reward of a man’s work rendered back to him, whether the work of a wicked man or of a good. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the standing rule in a line: God ever will do justice; the righteous shall never be forsaken, nor shall the wicked ultimately prosper. The verse is the counterpoise to the negative “far be it” of the verse before — God not only refrains from wrong but actively pays every man his due.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the connection and the grammar. The clause Elihu makes prominent is the very axiom the three friends defend, perfectly true in itself but falsely applied by them; here it is repeated, with the emphatic “yea verily” carried over into the next verse, as the assertion over against which Job’s complaint is measured. The verb for acting wickedly is read, as the sense requires, of God doing evil rather than being condemned as evil; and the proof of the whole, they note, will begin at v.13, with the question of who gave God his charge over the earth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the doctrine its pastoral reach. This is the standing rule of distributive justice, to give to every man according to his work: say to the righteous, it shall be well with them, and woe to the wicked, for it shall be ill with them. Good works shall be rewarded and evil works either punished or satisfied for, so that sooner or later, in this world or in the world to come, God will cause every man to find according to his ways. And Henry meets the obvious objection, that services now go unrewarded and sins now go unpunished, with the promise of a day of reckoning: there is a day coming when God will fully render to every man according to his works, with interest for the delay. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the active complement to divine justice, the guarantee that the God who cannot do wrong will also not fail to do right, and that the apparent disorders of the present are the deferrals, not the denials, of an exact and certain recompense.
12:
Elihu reaffirms his thesis with all the emphasis of an oath: yea surely, God will not do wickedly, neither will the Almighty pervert judgment. The reformed John Gill hears the truth repeated and affirmed in the strongest manner, and draws out a second sense from the versions: the Vulgate and the Targum render it “will not condemn,” that is, will not condemn the righteous. For though God may afflict his people, and does, it is that they may not be condemned with the world; there is no condemnation to them that are in Christ, whose righteousness secures them from every sentence. The negative “he will not pervert judgment” becomes, on this reading, a positive comfort to the afflicted believer, whose chastening is not the beginning of condemnation but its very opposite; the affliction of a saint, so far from being his condemnation, is the very means by which condemnation is kept from him.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds a single pointed word that shows where the emphasis bites: God will not pervert judgment, as Job hath affirmed. The force of Elihu’s asseveration lies in the charge it answers; he is not stating an abstract truth for its own sake but denying, under solemn assurance, precisely what he takes Job to have alleged, that God had dealt unjustly with him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the warmth of the assertion. It is asserted, first, with an assurance of its truth — yea, surely — a truth which none can deny or call in question, which we may take for granted and are all agreed in, that God will not do wickedly; and, second, with an abhorrence of the very thought of the contrary, so that to entertain the least suspicion of injustice in God, or to say anything that looks like charging him with it, is itself a thing to be put far away. Henry ties the assurance to the perfection of the divine nature: God will neither do any man wrong nor deny any man right, but the heavens will shortly declare his righteousness. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the sworn heart of Elihu’s answer, the flat and reverent denial that the God of perfect purity could ever swerve from justice — and Gill lifts it further, hearing in the promise that God will not condemn the very security of those whom, in love, he afflicts.
13:
To prove the impossibility of injustice in God, Elihu asks who gave him his charge over the earth, or who disposed the whole world. The reformed John Gill draws the argument out: is there any above God who committed the earth to him, made it his charge, and to whom he must give account? None at all. He is no deputy or sub-governor; the kings of the earth are under him, and he above the highest, sole Governor of the world in his own right, by right of creation, which he holds from himself and not another. Subordinate rulers sometimes do injustice to please a superior or through fear of one; but God has no superior to please and none to fear, and since he is the Judge of all the earth, he will do right.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same logic to the same end: where is God’s superior, who made the world and then delivered its government to him? God is the sole Creator and absolute Lord of all, and therefore cannot do unjustly, for the Creator must needs have all perfections in himself, and among them perfect justice. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps it plain — who governs and disposes the world but God, by his just and merciful providence, so that the government of the world itself displays his care, justice, and mercy.

The grammatical-historical voices attend to the wording of the second clause. Keil and Delitzsch fix the construction, rejecting Ewald’s “who searcheth” and Hahn’s “who careth for the earth beside him,” and take the verb to mean the enjoining of a charge, the entrusting of a duty. Charles Ellicott offers the two possible senses and shows that either serves: “who hath set the whole world upon him,” that is, entrusted it to his care, implying that none is over him; or “who but he hath made the whole world, and who therefore can have the interest in it that he must have?” Because the earth is his own and not another’s committed to him, his self-interest cannot collide with the welfare of his creatures. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a ground of submission: the government is his, and he does according to his will in all the hosts of heaven and earth; his power is original, of himself, and therefore if he be an absolute sovereign, we are bound to submit, for there is no higher power to which we may appeal.
14:
Elihu presses the argument from sovereignty to its edge: if God should set his heart upon man, and gather to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would fail at once. But the witnesses divide, and sharply, over the very sense of “set his heart.” The reformed John Gill reads it of hostile intent — not of God’s love and affections, but, as Jarchi adds, of a purpose to destroy: if God gives his mind to it and is set upon it, none can hinder him, and if he should severely mark and deal with men by the strictness of his justice, none could stand before him. That he does not, and that all have not long since perished, is itself the proof of how far he is from any injustice.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns the words the opposite way, reading them of God’s love: on whomsoever God sets his heart, that is, his love, though the body must perish and turn to dust like the rest of men, yet his soul will God gather to himself. The gathering of the spirit becomes, for Clarke, not a threat of ruin but a promise of salvation. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses the clause ambiguous and offers a third construction: “if he set his heart upon himself,” had regard to his own interest, then he would gather to himself his own spirit and breath — or else, supplying the “if,” the setting of his heart upon man is in a bad sense, to do him injury, in which case, since man is God’s own, God would only injure his own; and Ellicott adds that the writer of the closing clause can hardly have been ignorant of the dust of Gen. 3:19, and that Elihu’s speech is marked throughout by entire self-confidence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the reading of irresistible power: if God set his heart against man to ruin him, man’s spirit and breath would soon be gone, and all flesh perish together. Many men’s honesty, Henry notes, is owing purely to their impotency; but God, who is able to crush any man easily and suddenly, does not by arbitrary power crush any, and that forbearance must be ascribed to the infinite perfection of his nature. So the debate is real and threefold: whether “set his heart upon man” means a hostile purpose to destroy, as Gill and Henry take it, or God’s saving love that gathers the soul, as Clarke will have it, or God’s regard to his own interest in his own creatures, as Ellicott proposes — a single clause pulling toward wrath, toward mercy, and toward the divine self-consistency at once.
15:
The consequence of God’s recalling the breath is universal and instantaneous: all flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust. The reformed John Gill dwells on that word together — not one by one, or one after another, as men generally die, but all at once, as when the flood swept away the world of the ungodly. “All flesh” signifies all men, and their bodies of flesh in particular, weak, frail, and mortal; and if God do but gather or take out the spirit from them, they die immediately, which is here called perishing. The verse measures the whole race by the thread of a single sustaining breath.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the design of this verse and the last as one: to declare God’s absolute and uncontrollable sovereignty over all men. The argument is not merely that death is universal, but that the Author of life holds it wholly in his own hand, so that the continuance of every man from moment to moment is a pure dependence upon God. It is not merely that all men happen to die, but that the Living One upholds them, and may at any instant cease to uphold.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two sides of the truth with his usual care: what God can do with us, and what he may do without wronging us. He can soon bring us to dust; there needs no positive act of his omnipotence to do it, for if he do but withdraw the concurrence of his providence by which we live, and gather to himself that spirit and breath which was from his hand at first and is still in his hand, we expire immediately, like an animal in an air-pump when the air is exhausted. And this he may do without any injustice, for he does but recall the being he gave, of which we are but tenants at will, and which we have besides forfeited; so that, as long as it is continued to us of his mere favour, we have no reason to cry out of wrong, whatever other comforts are removed. The witnesses do not divide. They read the verse as the humbling floor of Elihu’s argument: that the very breath in which a man frames his complaints against God is God’s loan, revocable in a moment, and that a creature so held over the dust by the free hand of his Maker is in no position to arraign the justice by which he lives.
16:
Elihu turns from the company to Job himself, and puts an if upon his understanding: if now thou hast understanding, hear this, hearken to the voice of my words. The reformed John Gill is careful that this casts no slur on Job’s intelligence, for Job was a very understanding man, who had not lost his natural understanding by his afflictions, nor was he without an understanding of divine things, as his speeches show. The “if” is rather a taking for granted: if, or seeing, thou hast understanding, then hearken and attend. Gill records too the observation of some Jewish interpreters that the word is not a noun but an imperative verb — understand thou now, hear this — a call to take the matter into the heart and weigh it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, addressing this verse, sets out the two heads under which the whole following discourse to Job will run. There are two things Job is bidden to hear. First, that God is not to be quarrelled with for anything that he does; it is daring presumption to arraign and condemn the divine proceedings, as Job had done by his discontents. Second, that God is to be acknowledged and submitted to in all that he does; and to this end Elihu will urge divers considerations to beget in Job great and high thoughts of God, and so persuade him to proceed no further in his quarrel. The verse is the hinge on which the arbiter’s plea swings from doctrine to application.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch treat the opening as a call to attention framing the questions that follow, and carry the sense forward into the challenge Elihu is about to raise — whether one who hated right could govern at all, and whether Job will dare to condemn the All-just. The call to hear, on their reading, is inseparable from the challenge to think, for Elihu means to lead Job by his own understanding to a conclusion he cannot refuse. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the deliberate narrowing of the address. Elihu had spoken to the wise men as a company of judges; now he singles out the man whose cause is in question, and stakes the whole weight of what is to come on Job’s willingness to listen. It is at once a courtesy and a challenge: a courtesy, in crediting Job with the understanding to weigh the argument; a challenge, in implying that if Job will only think, he cannot but yield the point that God does no wrong.
17:
“Shall even he that hateth right govern?” — Elihu’s rhetorical question makes the very rule of the world a proof of the ruler’s justice, and the witnesses both defend the argument and probe its Hebrew. The reformed John Gill states the logic: one who hates moral and civil justice is unfit to rule among men, for to love and do righteousness is the qualification of a governor; and if God hated right, as he must seem to if he did it not, he would be unfit to govern the world as he does. To this absurdity, Gill says, Job is reduced by suggesting that right was not done him. He notes Broughton’s rendering, “can a foe to judgment rule well?” and a second possible sense of the verb, to bind, as a surgeon binds up a wound.

The wesleyan-arminian voices carry the same argument. Adam Clarke reads it, “shall he who hateth judgment lie under obligation,” or govern; it is preposterous that he who lives by no rule should impose rules on others, and God, the fountain of justice, binds man by his laws — wilt thou then condemn him who is the sum of righteousness? John Wesley makes Elihu’s reasoning one with Abraham’s in Gen. 18:25 and Paul’s in Rom. 3:5: if God were unjust, there would be nothing but injustice and confusion in the world; but we see a great deal of justice administered, and this must proceed from him who is the fountain of all justice, and he that makes men just shall not himself be unjust.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott states the argument in its strength and mends the last phrase. One who holds such a position of absolute rule cannot be other than most just: he who is fit to rule must be just, and he who is the ultimate ruler must be fit to rule, and therefore just; if he is absolutely just, how shall we condemn his government even when we cannot reconcile it with our view of right? And “him that is most just” is rather “him that is just and mighty,” not only just but able to execute justice because mighty. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds the humbling comparison: the righteous Lord so loves righteousness that, set beside him, even Job, though a perfect and upright man, might be said to hate right; shall such creatures as we prescribe to him, or condemn one who is righteous in all his ways? The witnesses converge on the argument while dividing only over the shading of a verb — whether the second clause turns on ruling, or on binding and obligation.
18:
Elihu argues from the reverence due to earthly rulers up to the reverence due to God: is it fit to say to a king, thou art wicked, and to princes, ye are ungodly? The reformed John Gill weighs the propriety carefully. It is not fit to say even to a bad king, thou art wicked; he may be reproved for his sins, but not by any and every one, and the Scriptural instances are of prophets sent in the name of the Lord, who did it with decency. Much less may it be said to a good king; and the word here, Belial, is a name for the worst of men and for the devil himself, signifying one without a yoke, lawless, or unprofitable — whereas a king is not lawless but a minister of God for good, for the punishment of evildoers and the praise of them that do well.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke insists on the sacredness of the office over the man. Civil governors should be treated with respect; no man should speak evil of the ruler of the people, and even where the man cannot be respected because his conduct is improper, the office itself is sacred and to be reverenced, for he who permits himself to rail against the man would destroy the office and authority if he could. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the rule tersely: though a king may be wicked, yet his subjects neither may nor dare call him so.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott names the form of the argument, an inference from the less to the greater: who could challenge a king or princes, and if not a king, how much less the King of kings? There is a strong ellipse in the Hebrew, but one naturally supplied. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the same movement its sting: it is more absurd and unbecoming to arraign God than to affront majesty and magistracy, which no king would bear; in favour of government we presume a sentence right unless the contrary be very evident, and it is not fit to tell a king to his face that he is wicked — Nathan reproved David by a parable. How absurd, then, to say so to God, and to impute iniquity to him who, having no respect of persons, is under no temptation to do an unjust thing. The witnesses do not divide over the argument, though a fine thread runs between them: Gill allows that a bad king may yet be reproved by the right person and in the right way, where Clarke and Wesley guard the office so jealously that subjects dare not call even a wicked king wicked.
19:
“Him that accepteth not the persons of princes, nor regardeth the rich more than the poor; for they all are the work of his hands” — the impartiality of God crowns the argument, and here a patristic voice joins the moderns. The latin-fathers Gregory the Great, in his exposition of Job, turns the verse to the searching of hearts: men esteem one another not for what they are in themselves but for what is accidental to them, so that in the accepting of persons we are swayed by what merely belongs to a man; but Almighty God examines conduct solely by the nature of its deserts, and often inflicts severer punishment for the very reason that he has given greater opportunities of serving him, as the Truth bears witness that to whom much is given, of him much shall be required, in Luke 12:48. By prince or tyrant, Gregory adds, may be understood every proud person, and by the poor the humble; God regards not the tyrant disputing against the poor, because in the judgment he knows not the proud who now oppress the life of the lowly.

The reformed John Gill states the plain doctrine: God is no respecter of the persons of any, not the greatest men on earth, kings and princes, but deals with them in his providence as with others, nor do they escape his wrath when they sin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the practical inference: if it be improper to speak against a king, how much more to speak disrespectfully of God, who is not influenced by human caprice and regards rich and poor alike, being equally his creatures and equally dependent on his providence.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the construction of the last clause and carry the thought into the sudden deaths that follow, reading God’s impartiality as grounded in the fact that prince and peasant are alike the work of his hands. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the comfort home to Job’s own case: rich and poor stand on the same level before God, a great man faring never the better for his wealth nor a poor man ever the worse for his poverty; Job, now that he is poor, should have as much favour with God, and be as much regarded, as when he was rich, for they are all the work of his hands — the poor made by the same hand and of the same mould as the rich, and made poor by the same providence that made others rich, so that they fare never the worse for what is their lot and not their fault. Gregory alone lifts the social terms into a figure of pride and humility; the rest keep them literal, but all four confess the same impartial Judge, with whom greatness buys no favour and lowliness suffers no loss.
20:
The impartial Judge proves his sovereignty over the greatest in the suddenness of their deaths: in a moment they die, at midnight the people are shaken and pass away, and the mighty are taken away without hand. The reformed John Gill spreads the leveling wide — princes as well as common people, rich as well as poor, kings and peasants, all must die, and sometimes suddenly, struck dead without previous notice, their souls required of them in an hour; he notes that the Targum refers the shaking at midnight to the men of Sodom. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse of Eastern tyrants, who seldom die a natural death: both mighty and poor depend alike on the Almighty for breath, and if the great abuse their power, God cuts them off by sudden and unexpected death, even at midnight, when they are least able to defend themselves, whether by the people they have oppressed or by the invisible hand of the angel of death.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the impartiality of the hour: they all alike die, rich and poor together, the hour of death neither hastened for the poor nor delayed for the rich. He thinks it hard to believe the writer did not know the midnight stroke of Exod. 12:29, and prefers to read the statements as habitual presents rather than futures — in a moment they die, even at midnight the people are shaken and pass away.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a meditation on God’s almighty ease. He is able to deal with the strongest of men when he enters into judgment: the people, the body of a nation, however numerous, may be troubled and unhinged when God pleases, and the mighty man, however honourable and formidable, if God speak the word, is taken from his throne, out of the land of the living, in a moment. It is no work of time with God to bring down his proud enemies; nor is he bound to give warning, no, not an hour’s. Henry too hears the midnight of the season, when men are secure and careless, as the Egyptians were when their firstborn were slain, and marks the manner — without hand, the immediate work of God by secret judgments, so that God can himself humble the greatest tyrant without the assistance of any man. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the proof that the God who accepts no persons needs no instruments, and that the loftiest are held over the grave by the same thread as the least.
21:
The sudden overthrow of the mighty rests on a deeper ground: God’s eyes are upon the ways of man, and he sees all his goings. The reformed John Gill unfolds the omniscience the words assert: it reaches every man, and all men, and their ways, every step they take, the whole of their lives and conversations, and every action of them, inward and outward. The inward, Gill suggests, may be intended in this clause and the outward in the next — all a man’s thoughts, the workings of his mind, the imaginations of his heart, his secret purposes and designs, the very desires and affections of his soul, and all of these whether good or bad, lie open before the eye of God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the attribute in its place in the argument: God is not only just and mighty but also all-wise, and therefore he cannot err. The sudden judgments of the verses before are no rash strokes, for they proceed from a knowledge that misses nothing. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the same conclusion toward the vindication of God’s justice: God does not destroy either prince or people unjustly, nor out of his mere pleasure, but for their sins, which he sees exactly, although they use all possible arts to hide them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the doctrine into a warning and a discipline. As the strongest cannot oppose God’s arm, so the most subtle cannot escape his eye; and therefore, if some are punished either more or less than we think they should be, instead of quarrelling with God it becomes us to ascribe it to some secret cause known to him only. Everything is open before him: his eyes are upon the ways of man, not merely so that they are within reach of his sight, but so that his eye is actually upon them, observing and inspecting; he sees us all and sees all our goings, and all our actions, good and evil, are regarded and recorded and reserved to be brought into judgment when the books shall be opened. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the hinge between God’s power and God’s justice, for the God who can crush the mighty in a moment does so as one who has read to the bottom every heart he judges, so that his severest providences, however dark to us, are the acts of a wisdom that cannot be deceived and a justice that cannot mistake its object.
22:
The reach of that all-seeing eye is stated in its extreme: there is no darkness, nor shadow of death, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves. The reformed John Gill takes the workers of iniquity chiefly for profane sinners who make a trade of sin, but includes the secret sinner and the hypocrite too; such may endeavour to hide themselves through shame or fear, but all in vain, for no darkness of any sort can hide them, neither the thick clouds of heaven nor the darkness of night, and there is no darkness in God himself to obstruct his sight, nor can they cast any mist before his eyes. Not even the shadow of death, the grave itself, is a hiding place, since from thence they shall be raised to receive the just deserts of their sins.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the two clauses a bolder, eschatological turn: there is no darkness in this life, and no shadow of death in the other world — no annihilation in which the workers of iniquity may take refuge. The grave affords no oblivion, and death opens no door of escape from the judgment of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the verse answering something Job himself had seemed to imply at ch. 24:13, where the murderer and the adulterer love the darkness and think themselves unseen; Elihu closes that supposed refuge.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse in its strophe and note that God makes short work with the mighty, without any process of investigation, for their conduct is at once manifest to him; the darkness that would screen a man from human courts is no screen from a Judge who needs no inquiry. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the terror and the folly of the attempt. The workers of iniquity would hide themselves, if they could, from the eye of the world for shame, and from the eye of God for fear, as Adam among the trees of the garden; they would gladly be hidden even by the shadow of death, buried in the grave and lying there for ever, rather than appear before the judgment-seat, so that the mighty men and chief captains will one day call to the rocks and mountains to hide them. But it is all in vain, for they may hide from men and never from God. The witnesses do not divide; Clarke alone lifts the shadow of death into the next world and denies the sinner even the refuge of annihilation, but all agree that no darkness, in this life or beyond it, can cover a man from the God whose eye has already found him out.
23:
God’s judgment is not only inescapable but exactly measured, for he will not lay upon man more than right, that he should enter into judgment with God. The reformed John Gill unfolds the moderation of it: God lays not more than right in a way of duty, his law being holy, just, and good, his yoke easy; nor in a way of punishment, always punishing less than iniquities deserve; nor in a way of chastisement, suffering nothing to befall his people but what is common to men, and bearing them up through it. Or, Gill allows, the words “than right” being a supplement, the clause may be joined to what follows and read of God’s not needing to appoint man a set time to come before him in judgment.

That second construction is where the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the meaning: God will not call man a second time into judgment, does not try a cause twice; his decisions are just and his sentence without appeal. On Mr. Good’s rendering, it is not to man that God has entrusted the time of coming into judgment with God; man’s lot is not ruled by his own wisdom, but when God thinks best he will judge for him and, if he is oppressed, bring forth his righteousness as the light.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays both readings side by side. The Authorized Version’s sense is probably right, that God lays not on man so much that he should enter into judgment with God; but some render, he needs not yet again to consider a man, that he should go before God in judgment — God having no need to consider any man’s case twice, or to rectify his first decision, being infallible and unable to do otherwise than right. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the plainer sense and turns it upon Job: even when God is overturning the mighty and breaking them in pieces, he will not lay upon man more than right, nor exact of the guilty more than their iniquities deserve, the proportion between sin and punishment being weighed by Infinite Wisdom; no man can enter into judgment with God or bring an action against him, for if he do, God will be justified when he speaks. Job, therefore, was much to be blamed for his complaints, and well-advised to let fall his action, which could only be cast. So a genuine divergence of rendering runs through the verse — whether it promises that God never punishes beyond desert, or that God, being infallible, needs no second trial of any man — and the witnesses hold both, agreeing at least that in neither sense has any man ground to arraign him.
24:
The measured Judge is also an irresistible one: he breaks in pieces mighty men without number, and sets others in their stead. The reformed John Gill catalogues the mighty God can shatter — mighty in bodily strength, like the giants of the old world, or in power and authority, kings and rulers, or in wealth — whom God breaks like potters’ vessels, and even whole kingdoms he makes as the chaff of the summer threshing-floor. The phrase, Gill notes, may be rendered “without number,” for there have been numberless such instances, or “without search,” meaning God needs no formal inquiry or examination of witnesses in a judicial process, all being naked and open before him at once. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the practical pattern: in multitudes of cases God depresses the proud and raises the humble, so that neither strength nor number affords the mighty any security.

The grammatical-historical voices prefer the second rendering. Keil and Delitzsch translate “he breaketh the mighty in pieces without investigation,” taking the word not as innumerabiles but as without research into their conduct, which is at once manifest to him. Charles Ellicott agrees: “without number” is rather “in an unsearchable manner,” as the “without hand” of v.20 — that is, without human means. So a genuine difference of reading opens beneath the verse: whether Elihu means that God breaks countless mighty men, as Gill’s first sense and the Authorized Version have it, or that he breaks them without any investigation or human agency, as the grammatical witnesses judge.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the plainer count while drawing out the providence: it is not one single mighty man that God can thus overpower, but even hosts of them, for no combined power can stand against Omnipotence. Yet, Henry adds, when God destroys tyranny he does not design anarchy; if those are brought down that ruled ill, it does not follow that a people must have no rulers, for when he breaks the mighty he sets others in their stead who will rule better — or, if they do not, he overturns them also, as the next verse will show. The witnesses do not finally divide over the truth that the mighty are as nothing before God; their quarrel is only over the shading of a single phrase, whether it counts the ruined or describes the searchless ease with which they are ruined, and both readings leave the throne of the world exactly where Elihu means it to rest, in the hand that raises and casts down at will.
25:
The overthrow of the mighty is the act of a knowledge that misses nothing: therefore he knoweth their works, and overturneth them in the night, so that they are destroyed. The reformed John Gill takes the knowing as more than bare omniscience, of which Elihu had already spoken; God rather takes notice of their works, weighs them, and makes them known — to the guilty themselves, fastening convictions on the conscience and obliging confession, as with Cain and Pharaoh; to others, by the judgments he executes, as on the old world and on Sodom; and to all at last, when every work shall be made manifest at the day of judgment. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on the suddenness of the nocturnal stroke: God knows what they have done and what they are plotting to do, and in the revolution of a single night the plenitude of power on which the day closed is annihilated, as in the case of Belshazzar and Babylon.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording, reading God’s seeing through their works as the ground of the overthrow he brings by night, and preferring, in the following clause, the sense that he strikes them in the very stead of evil-doers rather than merely on the place where such are punished. Charles Ellicott lingers on the opening word: we should expect “because” rather than “therefore,” but the writer, believing firmly in God’s justice, reasons the other way — since God acts thus in judgment, it follows that he knows the works of men and has just grounds for what he does.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weaves the same threads into the pattern of God’s dealings with tyrants. If God designs the mighty space to repent, he does not presently destroy them, but strikes them as wicked men with humbling judgments; if not, he overturns them in the night, and they are crushed — witness Belshazzar, whose kingdom was numbered and finished in a night. It is vain, Henry adds, to think of flying from God’s justice or absconding when his wrath is in pursuit, for the workers of iniquity may find means to hide themselves from men, but not from him who knows their works, both what they do and what they design. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the seam between omniscience and overthrow, where the God who reads every deed needs neither delay nor daylight to bring the mightiest down, and where the ruin that falls at midnight is only the outward form of a judgment already complete in the mind of God.
26:
When God strikes the mighty, he strikes them justly and openly: he smites them as wicked men in the open sight of others. The reformed John Gill lays the whole weight on that word “as wicked men,” for such is the strict justice of God that he never strikes or punishes men but as wicked men, and because of their wickedness. The casting of man out of Eden, the fall of the angels, the drowning of the old world, the destruction of Sodom, the ruin of Pharaoh, the driving out of the Canaanites, the captivities of Israel, and the everlasting punishment of the lost — all are of them as wicked men and for sin, so that God is not chargeable with any unrighteousness. Gill notes, with Sephorno, a second possible sense, “instead of wicked men,” illustrated by Pharaoh’s host shaken into the sea in the room of the Israelites.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses that second rendering as the better: “in the place of wicked men he striketh them,” that is, God executes his judgments in the sight of all beholders, striking down wicked men in their very place, so that there can be no doubt who are stricken or why. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause the same way — not “on the place where evil-doers are punished,” but taking and treating them in the evil-doers’ stead — and dwell on the vivid verb, which pictures a blow struck so that it resounds, the public smiting of those who had stood in unimpeachable honour.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the plainer sense but notes the openness: at times God executes his judgments more openly, and the mighty are suddenly destroyed in the sight of the people. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the purpose of the publicity: some humbling, mortifying judgments are brought upon the wicked rulers, and they are stricken as other wicked men are, as surely and as sorely, in their bodies, estates, or families; and this is done in terror, as an alarm to others, given in the open sight of all, that they too may see and fear and tremble before the justice of God. So a fine difference of rendering runs through the verse — whether God strikes them in the character of wicked men, marking the ground of the stroke, or in the place and stead of wicked men, marking its public and exemplary manner — and the witnesses divide gently between the two, agreeing that the blow, however read, is both righteous in its cause and open in its execution.
27:
Elihu names the reason the mighty are struck: because they turned back from him, and would not consider any of his ways. The reformed John Gill reads the turning back as apostasy from the ways and worship of God, as in the posterity of Cain before the flood and of Ham after it, who turned from the law of God, or, as the Septuagint has it, from the light and law of nature. The fault is not ignorance but defection, a deliberate turning of the back on a God once known. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the persons and the fault together: this is the reason God dealt with these corrupt and tyrannical rulers in judgment, for they had departed from him in their hearts, their moral conduct, and their civil government, and would not, would not, understand any of his ways.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes a pointed observation about Elihu’s own theology at this turn: “because they turned back from him” shows that Elihu, as well as Job’s other friends, believed in the direct execution of God’s judgments — the very doctrine of exact and visible retribution that the book as a whole is bringing into question. Elihu, for all his fresh manner, has not in fact climbed clear of the friends’ scheme. Keil and Delitzsch set the clause in its strophe as the ground of the falling away, carrying the sense into the cry of the oppressed poor that follows.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the anatomy of the sin most fully. To prove that God, in striking the mighty, does not lay upon them more than right, Elihu shows what their wickedness was; and these unjust judges, Henry says, neither feared God nor regarded man. They were rebels to God: they turned back from him, cast off the fear of him, and abandoned the very thoughts of him, for they would not consider any of his ways, taking no heed to his precepts or to his providences, but living without God in the world. This, Henry insists, is at the bottom of all the wickedness of the wicked, that they turn back from God; and it is because they will not consider, not because they cannot, so that from inconsideration comes impiety, and thence all immorality. The witnesses do not divide over the sin, though Ellicott hears in the verse a quiet exposure of the speaker: Elihu grounds the ruin of the mighty on their apostasy, and in doing so reveals that his own account of providence still runs on the friends’ line of visible reward and punishment, however broader the terms in which he casts it.
28:
The apostasy of the mighty shows itself in oppression, so that they cause the cry of the poor to come unto him, and he hears the cry of the afflicted. The reformed John Gill reads the plain movement of it: through the oppressions of tyrants the poor are made to cry, and they come to God with their cries and tears and supplications, which enter into the ears of the Lord of hosts. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the terror of it out with unusual warmth: these rulers were cruel and oppressive, the poor cried through their distresses and against their oppressors, and God heard; nothing appears so dreadful in the court of heaven against a hardhearted man of power as the prayers and tears and groans of the poor. Clarke tells the tale of a Scottish laird who persecuted his tenants for meeting to worship, until a plain, godly woman came and warned him that, if he would not let them alone, they would pray him dead; and the persecutor, not caring to put such prayers to the proof, wisely let them alone. When the poor refer their cause to God, Clarke concludes, he is a terrible avenger, and woe to the man that contendeth with his Maker.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the moral in a sentence: their case is bad who have the prayers and tears of the poor against them, for these will draw down vengeance, sooner or later, on the heads of their oppressors.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the same charge as the counterpart of the tyrants’ impiety. They will not call upon God for themselves, but they cause the cry of the poor to come to him, and that cry is against them; they are injurious and oppressive, wronging and crushing the poor, adding affliction to the afflicted, who make their complaint to God, and he hears them and pleads their cause. Their case is bad indeed who have the prayers and tears of the poor against them, for the cry of the oppressed will, sooner or later, draw down vengeance on the heads of the oppressors, as God had threatened in Exod. 22:23, and no one can say that this is more than right. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the hinge on which the sudden ruin of the mighty is made to hang, for the God who sees every deed and needs no inquiry has an ear especially open to the groan of the wronged, and the tyrant who stops that cry only sends it the surer to the throne of a Judge who will answer it in judgment.
29:
“When he giveth quietness, who then can make trouble? and when he hideth his face, who then can behold him?” — Elihu now sets God’s uncontrollable dominion over both nations and single men. The reformed John Gill spreads the quietness wide: peace is of God, external to communities and persons, and inward and spiritual in Christ, and when God gives it none can disturb it, neither the peace of a nation nor of a church nor of a single soul, which no affliction of the world nor temptation of Satan can break. He notes that the Targum and several versions read the clause “who shall condemn?” rather than “who shall make trouble?” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke calls the sentiment beautiful and true, and turns it into a plea for liberty of conscience: if God gives every man the right to worship according to his conscience, who shall dare say, worship in my way or not at all, or even, through a pretended liberality, offer to tolerate him on shackled terms? and he adds that God defends nations or individuals, however weak, against their enemies, however many, and destroys those who have filled up the measure of their iniquity.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the wording: literally the first clause is “who can condemn?” and the closing phrase is better “against a man alike,” meaning it is all one, for God judges nations as he judges individuals and individuals as he does nations. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in brief, that God can carry on his work of mercy or of justice as irresistibly upon a whole nation as upon one particular person.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two halves into a meditation on divine sovereignty. The frowns of all the world cannot trouble those whom God quiets with his smiles; when he gives quietness it is a challenge to all the powers of hell and earth to disquiet those to whom he speaks peace, so that neither the accusations of Satan nor the afflictions of this present time, nor even the arrests of death, can trouble the soul that dwells at ease in God, as the apostle promises in Phil. 4:7. And the smiles of all the world cannot quiet those whom God troubles, for if he hide his face, who can behold him, or see through the clouds that are round about him? none can relieve the distresses of the outward condition without God, as Elisha owned in 2 Kings 6:27. The witnesses divide only over a word — whether the clause reads “make trouble” or “condemn” — and agree wholly on the doctrine, that the same hand rules the fate of empires and of men, and that neither the many nor the mighty can add to or take from what God gives or withholds.
30:
“That the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared” — Elihu names the end God serves in all this overturning, and the witnesses read the hypocrite variously, one of them turning the charge back on Elihu himself. The reformed John Gill takes the hypocrite not for a common religious hypocrite but for a hypocrite in politics: one who pretends great humanity, a tender care of the people and their rights and liberties, and a zeal for religion, but who, once he has ascended the throne and got the power into his hands, throws off the mask and becomes a tyrant. Such men God either does not suffer to ascend, or, if they climb up by artifice, does not suffer to continue, but deposes and cuts them off. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the clause a broader turn, reading it of the provocation of God, whether on account of an ungodly man reigning or by the snares of a whole people — that is, the corruption of a nation, such as Sodom’s. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the reigning not of coming to the throne but of continuing the tyranny, God freeing the oppressed people from the snares that ungodly men lay for them; and Adam Clarke connects the Vulgate’s rendering, that God causes a wicked man to reign because of the sins of the people.

The latin-fathers Gregory the Great makes the most startling application, reading Elihu himself as a portrait of the haughty. Proud men, when they have said something they think praiseworthy, ask their hearers whether they have chanced to say anything amiss, not from any real doubt but to fish for approval; and so Elihu, after his many sublime sentiments, assumes an appearance of humility and, as though a disciple, addresses Job with a fair proposal — because I have spoken to God, I will not hinder thee; if I have sinned, teach thou me. For Gregory the very meekness of the coming verses is the hypocrite’s cloak.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the providence plainly: God is wise and careful of the public welfare, and provides that the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared. He notes the pride of hypocrites, who aim to reign, the policy of tyrants, who make religion a cloak for ambition, and the danger to a people under such rulers, whose liberties are more easily wheedled from them than forced; and against this danger divine Providence takes care that the hypocrite reign not at all, or not long, hastening the ruin of hypocritical rulers where God has mercy in store for a people. So the witnesses read the verse at two levels: most take it of the tyrant God will not let stand over the nations, while Gregory alone turns its light inward, upon the speaker whose show of humility is about to begin.
31:
“Surely it is meet to be said unto God, I have borne chastisement, I will not offend any more” — Elihu now stops rebuking and puts better words into Job’s mouth, and the witnesses receive the model penitent’s confession. The reformed John Gill marks that this is meet to be said by any afflicted person under God’s chastising hand, and particularly by Job, for whom the counsel is designed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the pastoral method: having reproved Job for his passionate words, Elihu directs him to what is good, that his reproof may be the reproof of instruction, as in Prov. 6:23; and he does not impose these words but recommends them. Unlike Job’s other friends, who would have had him own himself a wicked man and by overdoing undid, Elihu obliges him only to own that he had spoken unadvisedly with his lips. He directs Job first to humble himself and accept the punishment — I have borne chastisement; what I suffer comes justly upon me, and I will bear it, and not only justify God in it but acknowledge his goodness. Many are chastised, Henry observes, who do not bear chastisement well, and so in effect do not bear it at all; but a true penitent takes all well that God does, bearing it as a medicinal operation intended for good. And he directs Job, second, to promise reformation — I will not offend any more — binding himself with the bond of a fixed resolution never to return to folly.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums the whole in a breath: humble thyself before God, and say, I have suffered, I will not offend. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, however, render the opening clause otherwise, hearing not the words “I have borne chastisement” but a confession of pride, “I have been proud, I will not do evil” — so that even the model prayer carries a textual difficulty, whether the penitent owns the punishment he has borne or the pride that brought it. The witnesses do not divide over the substance of the confession, that it is meet for a chastened man to justify God, accept the rod, and resolve against sin; they part only over a word, whether Job is bidden to say that he has endured his stroke or that he has been proud. Either way the counsel is the same: the true end of affliction is a heart brought low enough to say to God, I take thy correction, and I will offend no more.
32:
The confession Elihu frames is completed by a prayer to be taught: that which I see not, teach thou me; if I have done iniquity, I will do no more. The reformed John Gill opens the words two ways. They may be understood of God’s chastisements and providential dealings, whose design and use are often unsearchable, so that a man may fitly say, it is but a small part of thy ways that I know; teach me more of thy mind and will in them. Or they may be understood of sins, so that an afflicted man says, I am conscious of many failings, but there may be secret sins that have escaped my notice; point them out to me, that I may be humbled for them and make a free confession. The wesleyan-arminian voices keep to the second sense. Adam Clarke renders it, what I do not know, teach thou me; wherein I have done iniquity, I will do so no more. John Wesley gives it in a line: the secret sins which I cannot discover, manifest thou to me.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the prayer as the desire of a good man to know the worst of himself. Job is to pray that God would discover his sins to him: Lord, upon the review I find much amiss in me and much done amiss by me, but I have reason to fear there is much more that I am not aware of, greater abominations, which through ignorance and self-partiality I do not yet see; Lord, give me to see it, and awaken my conscience to do its office faithfully. A good man, Henry says, is willing to know the worst of himself, and particularly under affliction desires to be told wherefore God contends with him and what God designs in correcting him.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the very posture of penitence, and it is worth noting that Job himself had already prayed in this key, when he begged, make me to know my transgression and my sin, and asked God to teach him what he could not see. Elihu here presses on Job the prayer Job had in substance already offered, so that the counsel, however sharply delivered, meets the sufferer on ground he had himself chosen: that the chastened heart does not defend its ignorance but asks to have its hidden faults brought into the light, resolving beforehand that whatever God shows it to have done amiss, it will do no more.
33:
Elihu confronts Job with the pride hidden in his discontent: should the recompense be according to thy mind, whether thou refuse or choose? The verse is famously abrupt, and the witnesses labour at both its sense and its obscurity. The reformed John Gill offers the alternatives: the words may respect the government of the world — is it fit that God, who made it, should consult men or be instructed by them? — or, nearer the context, chastisement — should a man be asked first whether he shall be chastened, or in what manner, as a son might be consulted by his father whether it is fitting to correct him? The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as a rebuke of Job’s presumption: does God need thy advice how to govern the world, and whom and when to reward or punish? and, if thou wilt not submit as bidden, therefore speak, if thou canst say anything for thyself, for I am ready to hear thy defence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confesses the verse obscure from its abruptness and presses its logic hard: should God recompense a man’s conduct according to thy mind, with thy concurrence, whether thou refusest or choosest? and if so, why not according as I refuse or choose, or as any man will? for if thou art to direct his government, so may I, so may anyone, and then he is no longer supreme or absolute. What knowest thou, then? Speak, if thou hast anything to say to this. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns the original obscure and offers Mr. Good’s paraphrase — according as thou art bruised shall he make thee whole, but it is thine to choose, not mine — pressing Job to determine whether he will humble himself under the mighty hand of God or persist in his supposed integrity, and then to say so.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reasons with Job’s uneasiness under affliction. We are ready to think everything that concerns us should be just as we would have it, but Elihu shows it absurd to expect this: should it be according to thy mind? No; must we never be afflicted because we have no mind to it? is it fit that everything be according to God’s mind, and not ours, for he is the Creator and we the creatures, he in one mind and we in many. And it is vain as well as absurd, for he will recompense it whether thou refuse or choose; God will take his own way, and it is therefore thy wisdom to be easy, to make a virtue of necessity, and to be at a point, for thou art in God’s hand. The witnesses do not divide over the thrust of the verse, that God’s government and recompense are not to be bent to a man’s private will; they only confess, with Ellicott and Clarke, that its very words are among the hardest in the chapter to construe.
34:
Elihu appeals over Job’s head to the discerning who are listening: let men of understanding tell me, and let a wise man hearken unto me.
