The reformed John Gill takes it as a simple submission of his case, whether he is right or wrong, to men of judgment; he is willing, that is, that his own words be tried by the very assay he had laid down at the opening of the speech, that the ear tries words as the palate tastes its food. The wesleyan-arminian voices read it the same way. Adam Clarke: I wish to converse with wise men, and by men of wisdom I wish what I have said to be judged; John Wesley: I am content that any wise man should judge of my words, and let such consider what I say.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, alters the mood of the verb and so the confidence of the appeal. It is rather, he says, men of understanding will say to me, or will agree with me, and every wise man that hears me will say — not a request that the wise judge his cause, but a claim that they already side with him. The difference is not slight: on Gill’s reading Elihu humbly submits his words to the verdict of the discerning; on Ellicott’s he presumes that verdict in advance, taking the assent of all wise men for granted, and Keil and Delitzsch, setting the verse at the head of the closing appeal, carry the same self-assurance into the sharp sentence that follows, that Job has spoken without knowledge.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the appeal to the bystanders as a request that they weigh the construction he has put upon Job’s words: let men of understanding tell me whether they can put any more favourable construction upon what Job has said than I have put, and whether he has not spoken very ill and ought not to cry, I have done wrong. So the verse gathers a genuine, if quiet, difference of grammar with a difference of tone: whether Elihu, at the close, humbly refers his charge to the judgment of the wise, as the reformed and Wesleyan witnesses take him, or whether, as the grammatical witnesses judge, he anticipates their agreement and speaks already as one sure the whole company of the discerning is on his side. The one reading leaves Elihu a suppliant for a fair verdict; the other shows him a man who has, in his own mind, already won it, and who summons the wise less to try his case than to confirm it.
35:
The verdict Elihu invites is a sharp one: Job has spoken without knowledge, and his words were without wisdom. The reformed John Gill is careful to bound the charge. It is not that Job was an ignorant man, whether in things natural or divine, but that in this one point, about the chastening hand of God upon him, he had said things that betrayed a lack of knowledge. The censure falls on Job’s speech in the controversy, not on his character or his general understanding. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it more roundly, and with less patience: there is no good arguing with a self-willed, self-conceited man, and Job has spoken like one destitute of wisdom and discretion.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the sentence as the words the wise men are made to say of Job — Job speaketh without knowledge, and his words are without intelligence — and set it at the head of the closing indictment that runs to the end of the chapter, in which Elihu asks that Job be tried to the utmost for answering after the manner of evil men. The verdict is put, that is, not as Elihu’s private opinion only but as the judgment he expects every discerning hearer to pronounce.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the charge and finds it, in this matter, just, though he softens it as Gill does. Elihu cannot say that Job is without knowledge and wisdom in general; but in this business Job has spoken without knowledge, and, whatever his heart, his words were without prudence. And Henry turns Job’s own words back upon him with a neat stroke: what Job had once said to his wife may here be retorted upon himself, that he now speaks as one of the foolish men speak, and for the same reason — shall we not receive evil as well as good at God’s hand, as Job had rebuked her in ch. 2:10? Sometimes, Henry observes, we need and deserve the very reproofs we have given to others, and those who reproach God’s wisdom really reproach their own. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether they bound the fault narrowly to Job’s speech in the trial, as Gill and Henry do, or press it more severely against the man, as Clarke does, all agree that the censure touches not Job’s wisdom at large but the unadvised words in which, under the rod, he had reflected on the government of God.
36:
Elihu’s wish for Job hardens into a demand that his trial be pressed to the end, because of his answers for wicked men. The reformed John Gill gives it as Elihu’s own opinion, brought forward and left with the men of understanding, but notes that some, with Broughton, render the opening not “my desire” but “O my Father, let Job be tried,” turning the clause into an address to God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott prefers that marginal reading, taking the words as spoken to God — O my Father, let Job be tried — and adds that Elihu’s words cannot have fallen upon Job with more acceptance, or less weight, than those of his other friends, since Job must have felt his cause safe with God whatever the misunderstanding of men. Ellicott also mends the last clause: not “his answers for wicked men,” but rather his answering like wicked men.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley holds the other rendering of that clause, that Job be tried thoroughly, until the cause be brought to an issue, because of his answers on behalf of wicked men, into whose mouths he has, in Wesley’s view, put arguments against God and his providence. But Adam Clarke recoils from the whole verse. He too notes the reading “My father, let Job be tried,” and Mr. Good’s harsher “let Job be pursued to conquest for replying like wicked men,” and then delivers his verdict on Elihu: this is a very harsh wish, and the whole chapter is in the same spirit, nearly destitute of mildness and compassion. Who could suppose, Clarke asks, that such arguings could come from the mouth of the loving Saviour of mankind? — recalling, with plain incredulity, that a very pious divine had actually supposed Elihu to be Jesus Christ.

So the verse holds two divisions at once. There is the textual and grammatical division, over whether Elihu says “my desire” or cries “O my Father,” and whether Job answered for wicked men or like them; and there is the deeper division of judgment, between those who take Elihu’s demand as the sober close of a well-meant reproof and Clarke, who hears in it only cruelty, a wish to prolong a broken man’s affliction that ill suits an arbiter professing to plead God’s cause. The witnesses part company here as nowhere else in the chapter, not over the meaning of a word only, but over the very spirit of the speaker.
37:
“For he addeth rebellion unto his sin” — Elihu closes his charge at its sharpest, that Job clappeth his hands among the company and multiplieth his words against God; and here the witnesses divide most deeply over whether the charge is just. The reformed John Gill softens it into a warning, reading the verb as “he may” or “will add”: as yet Job has committed, it may be charitably hoped, only sins of ignorance and mistake, but if he is let alone and not stopped he will proceed from evil to evil, to presumptuous sins and open rebellion against God. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the charge as standing: Job sinned before by impatience under his afflictions, and now, grown obstinate, instead of humbling himself he justifies himself and accuses the blessed God; his clapping of the hands is insulting and triumphing, and his multiplied words are against God, in effect though not directly.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, by contrast, turns the whole force of his comment against Elihu. The charge is an ill-natured, cruel, and unfounded assertion, borne out by nothing Job had ever said or intended, and more severe than the most inveterate of his other friends had spoken; there was no need of adding such a caustic, for Elihu, who began well and tolerantly, has by now got fairly into the spirit and under the mistake of those who preceded him in this tempest of words. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses only the gesture, that Job clappeth his hands among them as though confident of victory in argument.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets out the three-fold indictment as Elihu means it. If Job’s words be tried to the end, they will be found, first, to take part with God’s enemies, his answers tending to strengthen the hands and harden the hearts of the wicked; second, to insult God’s friends, for to clap the hands and triumph as if error and passion had won the victory is worse than to speak ill; and third, to speak against God himself, and, by standing to what he had said, to add rebellion to his sin — for to speak even one word against God is a great sin, and what is it to multiply words against him, as if a man would out-talk his Maker? Henry closes with the old confession that measures the whole: I may fall into error, but I will not plunge into heresy. So the chapter ends on a real and unresolved division: Gill hears a caution against a rebellion not yet reached, Wesley and Henry a fair naming of Job’s obstinacy, and Clarke a cruel and groundless caustic unworthy of one who professed to plead for God — the arbiter’s last word falling, in Clarke’s ear, harder than any blow the friends had struck.
